newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil posts $413 mln Jan trade gap.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil posts $413 mln Jan trade gap.

text.p: Following are economists' comments on Brazil's $413 million January trade gap, which reportedly included $534 million in fuel imports.

THOMAS MALAGA, economist at Brazilian retail bank Unibanco: "We estimate that January imports were probably about $300 million more than was reported because of problems with (the government's new import registry) Siscomex. These imports will be passed on this month so we see February's trade deficit rising to about $1.0 billion from $600 million."
Malaga said problems with Siscomex might not be fully worked out until March and that true monthly trade figures would not be available until April.

He added that Brazil, which last posted a trade surplus in May 1996, would probably not see another surplus until May even though the nation begins exporting the bulk of its agricultural output in March.
"We think there will be a surplus in May. It would be difficult to have a surplus in April," Malaga said.
CLIVE BOTELHO, executive director at Brazilian investment bank Banco BMG: "The figure was a positive surprise."
Botelho added, "It indicates that January oil imports were lower than expected and the amount of imports that will be carried over to February due to problems in Siscomex will also be lower."
The government reported Wednesday that fuel imports for the month might come in at $650 million. Instead, they reportedly totaled $534 million.
Botelho said the bank forecasts a $1.0 billion trade gap in February, which he said would include about $300 million in imports that were not registered by Siscomex in January.

NILSON TEIXEIRA, chief economist at Rio de Janeiro investment bank Fonte Cindam: "We don't know whether this figure really reflects total imports in January or if problems in Siscomex prevented imports from being registered and therefore will only come up in February's data."
Teixeira said the market will not know Brazil's actual trade performance in January and February until March, when most of the start-up problems with Siscomex should be resolved.
Brazil posted a record $5.5 billion trade deficit in 1996, which is expected to rise to about $8.0 billion this year.
